questiontext.text:
Consider the following five statements regarding respiratory mechanisms across different animal groups:

(a) Sponges, coelenterates, and flatworms exchange gases by simple diffusion over their entire body surface.
(b) Earthworms utilise their moist cuticle for the exchange of respiratory gases.
(c) Insects possess a network of tracheal tubes to transport atmospheric air within the body.
(d) Aquatic arthropods and molluscs respire exclusively through vascularised bags called lungs.
(e) Adult frogs can undergo gaseous exchange through their moist skin as well as through lungs.

Which of the following options correctly identifies all the true statements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of lower invertebrate respiration
Lower invertebrates such as sponges, coelenterates, and flatworms lack specialised respiratory organs; they exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide by simple diffusion across their entire body surface.

Step 2: Evaluation of annelid and insect mechanisms
Earthworms use their moist, thin cuticle for cutaneous respiration, whereas insects possess an extensive tracheal system (network of tubes) that distributes atmospheric air directly to tissues.

Step 3: Evaluation of aquatic arthropod and mollusc respiration
Aquatic arthropods and molluscs use specialised vascularised structures termed gills (branchial respiration), whereas vascularised bags called lungs are characteristic of terrestrial forms.

Step 4: Evaluation of amphibian respiration
Amphibians such as frogs demonstrate pulmonary respiration via lungs as well as cutaneous respiration through their moist skin.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The accurate statements are those affirming diffusion across the entire body surface in lower invertebrates, moist cuticular respiration in earthworms, tracheal network in insects, and dual cutaneous-pulmonary respiration in frogs, whereas attributing lungs to aquatic arthropods and molluscs is incorrect. Thus, statements (a), (b), (c), and (e) are true.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CLASS11_CH14_STATEMENT_Q02 - Anatomy of the human respiratory system

questiontext.text:
Read the following five statements concerning the human respiratory tract and thoracic chamber:

(a) The trachea divides into right and left primary bronchi at the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra.
(b) Incomplete cartilaginous rings support the trachea, primary, secondary, and tertiary bronchi, as well as terminal bronchioles.
(c) The conducting part extends from external nostrils up to the terminal bronchioles, clearing, humidifying, and conditioning incoming air.
(d) The outer pleural membrane is in close contact with the pulmonary surface, while the inner pleural membrane lines the thoracic cavity.
(e) The thoracic chamber is anatomically formed dorsally by the vertebral column, ventrally by the sternum, laterally by ribs, and inferiorly by the dome-shaped diaphragm.

Which of the following options represents the collection of all correct statements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Assessment of tracheal branching
The trachea is a straight tube running through the neck into the mid-thoracic cavity, where it bifurcates at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi.

Step 2: Assessment of cartilaginous ring distribution
Incomplete cartilaginous rings support the trachea, primary, secondary, and tertiary bronchi, and initial bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles do not possess these supporting rings.

Step 3: Assessment of conducting zone functions
The conducting zone extends from the external nostrils to the terminal bronchioles. It transports atmospheric air to alveoli, clears inhaled dust and foreign debris, humidifies the air, and equilibrates air temperature to body temperature.

Step 4: Assessment of pleural membranes
The double-layered pleura surrounds the lungs: the outer pleural membrane is in close contact with the thoracic lining, whereas the inner pleural membrane is in contact with the lung surface.

Step 5: Assessment of thoracic boundary anatomy
The thoracic cage is an airtight compartment bounded dorsally by the vertebral column, ventrally by the sternum, laterally by the ribs, and on the lower side by the dome-shaped diaphragm.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
Only the statements describing tracheal bifurcation, the boundaries and roles of the conducting part, and the boundaries of the thoracic chamber are valid. The statements regarding terminal bronchiole rings and the inversion of pleural membrane positions are erroneous. Therefore, statements (a), (c), and (e) are correct.

questiontext.text:
Analyze the following five statements regarding the biomechanics of pulmonary ventilation in humans:

(a) Inspiration is initiated by the contraction of the diaphragm, which increases thoracic volume in the antero-posterior axis.
(b) Contraction of external intercostal muscles lifts the ribs and sternum, increasing thoracic volume in the dorso-ventral axis.
(c) An overall increase in thoracic volume creates positive intra-pulmonary pressure relative to atmospheric pressure, driving air inwards.
(d) Expiration under normal quiet breathing is a passive event caused by the relaxation of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles.
(e) Additional abdominal muscles can be recruited to augment the strength of both inspiration and expiration.

Which of the following combinations contains all the correct statements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of diaphragmatic action during inspiration
Contraction of the dome-shaped diaphragm flattens it, thereby expanding the thoracic cavity along the antero-posterior axis.

Step 2: Evaluation of intercostal action during inspiration
Contraction of the external intercostal muscles elevates the ribs and sternum outward and upward, enlarging the thoracic chamber in the dorso-ventral axis.

Step 3: Evaluation of intrapulmonary pressure gradient
An increase in pulmonary volume causes a fall in intra-pulmonary pressure below atmospheric pressure (creating negative intra-pulmonary pressure), which draws atmospheric air into the lungs. Positive intra-pulmonary pressure would expel air, not draw it in.

Step 4: Evaluation of relaxation during quiet expiration
Quiet expiration occurs when the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax, returning the ribs, sternum, and diaphragm to their resting positions, compressing thoracic volume and elevating intra-pulmonary pressure above atmospheric levels.

Step 5: Evaluation of accessory muscle recruitment
Humans can increase the force and depth of respiratory movements during forced breathing using additional muscles, such as abdominal muscles and internal intercostals.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The accurate statements are those detailing antero-posterior expansion via the diaphragm, dorso-ventral expansion via external intercostals, passive recoil during quiet expiration, and voluntary capacity enhancement via abdominal muscles. The assertion stating that inspiration involves positive intra-pulmonary pressure is false. Hence, statements (a), (b), (d), and (e) are correct.

questiontext.text:
Given below are five statements concerning human respiratory volumes and diagnostic pulmonary capacities:

(a) Tidal volume is approximately \(500\text{ mL}\), providing a minute ventilation of \(6000\) to \(8000\text{ mL}\) in a healthy adult.
(b) Residual volume averages \(1100\text{ mL}\) to \(1200\text{ mL}\) and cannot be directly measured by a standard spirometer.
(c) Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) represents the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a forced expiration.
(d) Vital Capacity (VC) is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration, mathematically equal to \(\mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV}\).
(e) Total Lung Capacity equals Vital Capacity minus Residual Volume (\(\mathrm{VC} - \mathrm{RV}\)).

Which of the following options identifies all the correct statements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Tidal Volume and ventilation rate
Tidal volume is the volume of air inspired or expired in a normal breath (about \(500\text{ mL}\)). At a resting rate of \(12\text{--}16\text{ breaths/min}\), total minute volume is \(500 \times 12 = 6000\text{ mL}\) to \(500 \times 16 = 8000\text{ mL}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Residual Volume
Residual volume is the volume remaining in the lungs even after a maximal, forcible expiration, averaging \(1100\text{--}1200\text{ mL}\). Because it remains permanently trapped in alveolar spaces, it cannot be expelled or measured directly by spirometry.

Step 3: Evaluation of Functional Residual Capacity
Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is defined as the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal, quiet expiration. It equals \(\mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV}\). Residual volume alone remains after a forced expiration.

Step 4: Evaluation of Vital Capacity
Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air an individual can inhale following a maximal expiration (or exhale following a maximal inspiration). Its formula is \(\mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV}\).

Step 5: Evaluation of Total Lung Capacity
Total lung capacity is the entire volume of air present in the lungs at the end of a forced inspiration, which is given by \(\mathrm{VC} + \mathrm{RV}\) (or \(\mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV} + \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV}\)), not their difference.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The accurate statements are those defining tidal volume and its minute output, residual volume, and vital capacity. The statements defining functional residual capacity (confusing normal expiration with forced expiration) and total lung capacity (subtracting rather than adding residual volume) are incorrect. Hence, statements (a), (b), and (d) are correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CLASS11_CH14_STATEMENT_Q05 - Gas exchange gradients and diffusion membrane

questiontext.text:
Examine the following five statements regarding alveolar gas exchange and the diffusion membrane:

(a) The \(\mathrm{pO_2}\) in alveolar air is \(104\text{ mm Hg}\), while in deoxygenated blood entering pulmonary capillaries it is \(40\text{ mm Hg}\).
(b) The \(\mathrm{pCO_2}\) in deoxygenated blood is \(45\text{ mm Hg}\), whereas in alveolar air it is \(40\text{ mm Hg}\).
(c) The solubility of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is \(20\text{ to }25\) times higher than the solubility of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in biological membranes.
(d) The diffusion membrane consists of three microscopic layers: alveolar squamous epithelium, capillary endothelium, and the intervening basement substance.
(e) The total thickness of the diffusion membrane exceeds \(2\text{ mm}\), preventing fluid extravasation into alveoli.

Which of the following options correctly lists all the true statements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of oxygen partial pressure gradients
Alveolar \(\mathrm{pO_2}\) is \(104\text{ mm Hg}\) and that of incoming systemic deoxygenated blood is \(40\text{ mm Hg}\), establishing a steep partial pressure difference of \(64\text{ mm Hg}\) driving oxygen into blood.

Step 2: Evaluation of carbon dioxide partial pressure gradients
Deoxygenated blood has a \(\mathrm{pCO_2}\) of \(45\text{ mm Hg}\) and alveolar air has \(40\text{ mm Hg}\), producing a gradient of \(5\text{ mm Hg}\) facilitating carbon dioxide movement into alveoli.

Step 3: Evaluation of gas solubilities
The solubility of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is \(20\text{--}25\) times greater than that of \(\mathrm{O_2}\), enabling high rates of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) diffusion across the barrier despite a smaller partial pressure difference.

Step 4: Evaluation of membrane layers
The respiratory diffusion membrane consists of three structural layers: the thin, single-layered squamous epithelium of the alveoli, the single-cell capillary endothelium, and the non-cellular basement substance between them.

Step 5: Evaluation of membrane thickness
The total thickness of the respiratory diffusion barrier is much less than a millimetre (fractions of a micrometre), optimising rapid gaseous diffusion.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The accurate statements are those citing correct partial pressures for oxygen and carbon dioxide, and describing the three anatomical layers of the diffusion membrane. The statements claiming higher oxygen solubility and a thickness greater than two millimetres are incorrect. Therefore, statements (a), (b), and (d) are true.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CLASS11_CH14_STATEMENT_Q06 - Gas transport and neural control mechanisms

questiontext.text:
Read the following five statements regarding the transport of gases and neural regulation of respiration:

(a) Every \(100\text{ mL}\) of oxygenated blood delivers approximately \(5\text{ mL}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) to tissues under normal physiological conditions.
(b) Nearly \(70\%\) of carbon dioxide is transported as bicarbonate ions (\(\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\)), a conversion catalysed predominantly by carbonic anhydrase in RBCs.
(c) High \(\mathrm{pCO_2}\), low \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and low temperature at the alveolar surface facilitate dissociation of oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin.
(d) The pneumotaxic centre in the pons region can reduce the duration of inspiration and thereby alter respiratory rate.
(e) Oxygen concentration in arterial blood plays the primary dominant role in activating central and peripheral chemoreceptors to set the basal respiratory rhythm.

Which of the following options includes all the correct statements?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of oxygen delivery to tissues
Under normal resting physiological conditions, every \(100\text{ mL}\) of arterial oxygenated blood releases roughly \(5\text{ mL}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) to peripheral body tissues.

Step 2: Evaluation of carbon dioxide forms of transport
Carbon dioxide is transported in three ways: about \(70\%\) as bicarbonate ions (\(\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\)) formed via high concentrations of carbonic anhydrase within RBCs, \(20\text{--}25\%\) as carbamino-haemoglobin, and about \(7\%\) dissolved in plasma.

Step 3: Evaluation of alveolar conditions for oxyhaemoglobin
In alveoli, high \(\mathrm{pO_2}\), low \(\mathrm{pCO_2}\), lower \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration (higher pH), and lower temperature favour the binding of oxygen to haemoglobin (oxyhaemoglobin formation), not dissociation.

Step 4: Evaluation of the pneumotaxic centre
The pneumotaxic centre located in the pons sends inhibitory impulses to the medullary rhythm centre, limiting the duration of inspiration and modulating respiratory rate.

Step 5: Evaluation of oxygen in chemoreceptor regulation
The respiratory rhythm centre and adjacent chemosensitive area in the medulla, as well as peripheral receptors in the carotid and aortic bodies, are sensitive to \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ion levels. The direct role of oxygen in regulating normal respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant.

Step 6: Final Conclusion
The accurate statements are those confirming the volume of oxygen delivered per \(100\text{ mL}\) of blood, the predominant bicarbonate transport mechanism, and the role of the pontine pneumotaxic centre. The assertions regarding factors promoting alveolar dissociation and oxygen dominating rhythm regulation are incorrect. Thus, statements (a), (b), and (d) are correct.
